usage: 보일러가 고장났어요
The boiler broke down
The exact line to open a call to your 집주인 (landlord) about heating
또 고장났어
It broke again
Casual gripe to a roommate; 또 = again, very common in real complaints
고장 난 것 같아요
It seems to be broken
고장 + 나다 written apart; -ㄴ 것 같다 hedges it as a guess, sounds polite
엘리베이터가 자주 고장나요
The elevator breaks down often
자주 = often; a recurring-problem report for the 관리실
examples: 에어컨이 고장나서 너무 더워요.
The AC broke down so it's really hot.
고장나서 = because it broke; the cause clause leads into the result
세탁기가 고장난 것 같아요.
I think the washing machine is broken.
-ㄴ 것 같다 softens it to a guess, polite for first reporting a problem
휴대폰이 갑자기 고장났어요.
My phone suddenly broke.
갑자기 = suddenly, the natural adverb for an out-of-nowhere malfunction
nuance: 고장나다 is built from the Sino-Korean noun 고장 (故障, 'breakdown/fault') plus native 나다 ('to occur'), so it literally means 'a fault arises' — which is why it is intransitive: the machine breaks on its own and takes 이/가, never 을/를 (보일러가 고장났어요, not 보일러를). Use it for things with a mechanism — appliances, electronics, cars, elevators — not for soft objects that simply tear or wear out (옷이 찢어지다, 신발이 닳다). The near-synonym 망가지다 is broader and casual ('get wrecked/ruined') and can cover a smashed toy or a crumpled box, whereas 고장나다 specifically implies the function stopped working. The English-speaker trap: English lets a person 'break' something, but you cannot make 고장나다 transitive — to say a PERSON broke it, switch to 고장 내다 or 망가뜨리다 (동생이 리모컨을 고장 냈어요).

mistakes: Saying 'X을/를 고장났어요' — 고장나다 takes 이/가, not 을/를, because the broken thing is the subject that the fault 'arose in', not an object you act on.

Stretching it to torn clothes or a ripped bag — those are 찢어지다, not 고장나다, which needs a working mechanism to fail.

usage: 수리해 주세요
Please fix it
What you say to a repair person or building manager (관리실)
수리 맡겼어요
I dropped it off for repair
수리 맡기다 = leave it to be fixed, e.g. a phone at the 서비스센터
수리비가 얼마예요?
How much is the repair cost?
수리비 (修理費) = repair fee; the first question at any service counter
수리 받아야 돼요
It needs to get repaired
수리(를) 받다 = receive a repair; the appliance is treated as needing service
examples: 보일러를 수리해야 돼요.
I need to get the boiler repaired.
Object takes 을/를 here, unlike 고장나다 which takes 이/가
냉장고를 수리하는 데 얼마예요?
How much does it cost to repair the fridge?
-는 데 = the cost/effort of doing; the go-to frame for asking a quote
기사님이 내일 수리하러 오신대요.
They say the technician is coming to repair it tomorrow.
기사님 = service technician; -신대요 relays what the 관리실 told you
nuance: 수리하다 comes from 수리 (修理, 'mend-manage') and is the formal, on-the-invoice word for repair — you see it on signs, receipts, and in 수리비 (repair cost) and 수리 기사 (repair technician). Its everyday near-synonym 고치다 is native Korean and warmer: a friend 고쳐 줄게 ('I'll fix it for you'), but a service center 수리합니다. The dividing line is register and scale: 고치다 covers a quick DIY tweak or even fixing a habit (버릇을 고치다), while 수리하다 implies a professional working on machinery, a car, or a building, and it stays strictly physical. The English-speaker trap: 'fix' in English also means to fix a plan, a date, or a relationship — none of those take 수리하다. A relationship or a problem is 관계를 회복하다 / 문제를 해결하다, and setting a date is 날짜를 정하다, so reserve 수리하다 for objects that physically broke.

Saying just 수리해 to a stranger technician — add 주세요 (수리해 주세요); the bare 해 form is reserved for close, casual relationships.

usage: 설치해 주세요
Please install it
Say this when a delivery crew brings an appliance or you order internet
설치 기사님 오셨어요
The installation technician is here
설치 기사 = install tech; constant with 인터넷/에어컨 setups
설치비 따로 있어요?
Is there a separate installation fee?
설치비 (設置費) = install charge; ask before the crew starts
앱 설치했어요
I installed the app
설치하다 covers software too; the casual chore-done report
examples: 에어컨을 설치하러 왔어요.
I came to install the air conditioner.
Said by the technician; -러 오다 = come in order to do
이 앱을 설치하면 가스비를 낼 수 있어요.
If you install this app, you can pay the gas bill.
Software sense; -면 = if/when you do, then the result follows
인터넷을 언제 설치할 수 있어요?
When can you install the internet?
The key question when setting up a brand-new apartment
nuance: 설치하다 is from 설치 (設置, 'set up-place') and means putting equipment in and making it ready to run — air conditioners, shelves, a washing machine, CCTV — as well as installing software and apps. The dividing line against the plain native verb 놓다 ('put/place') is readiness: 놓다 just sets an object somewhere, while 설치하다 implies mounting, wiring, or configuring it into working order. Watch the sibling word 설정하다 (設定, 'configure'): you 설치 the app or the router first, then 설정 the options inside it — English 'set up' blurs these two, but Korean keeps them apart. The other English-speaker trap is 'uninstall': there is no 설치 취소; Koreans say 삭제하다 ('delete') or 지우다 for software and 철거하다/떼다 for physically removing fixtures, so don't try to negate 설치하다 to undo it.

Using 놓다 when you mean a real installation — 에어컨을 놓다 sounds like you just set the unit on the floor, not that it was mounted and wired to work.

usage: 방 좀 정리해
Tidy up your room a bit
Classic line from a parent or roommate; 좀 softens the command
책상 정리했어요
I organized my desk
정리하다 + a space noun = arrange that specific area neatly
생각 좀 정리하고 올게요
Let me gather my thoughts and come back
생각을 정리하다 = sort out your thinking; works on abstract things too
짐 다 정리했어요
I've sorted out all my stuff
짐 = belongings/luggage; 다 = all of it, fully done
examples: 주말에 옷장을 정리할 거예요.
I'm going to organize my closet this weekend.
A common weekend chore; 옷장 = wardrobe/closet
냉장고를 정리하니까 공간이 많아졌어요.
After I organized the fridge, there's more space.
-니까 here = doing it and then noticing the result that follows
짐을 다 정리하고 나서 쉬었어요.
I rested after I finished sorting all my stuff.
-고 나서 = after completely finishing the prior action
nuance: 정리하다 is from 정리 (整理, 'arrange-manage') and means putting things into order so a space (or even a thought) looks settled and neat. Compare three neighbors learners blur: 치우다 emphasizes clearing things AWAY/out of sight, 청소하다 (淸掃) is removing dirt by sweeping/wiping/vacuuming, and 정리하다 is arranging what stays into proper order. So you can have a 정리된 (well-arranged) desk that is still dusty, because 정리 is about order, not cleanliness. A real strength of 정리하다 is that it also takes abstract objects: 생각을 정리하다 (collect your thoughts), 일정을 정리하다 (sort out a schedule), 관계를 정리하다 (end/wrap up a relationship). The English-speaker trap is mapping 'clean up' straight onto 정리하다 — if you mean wiping grime or mopping, that is 청소하다/닦다, not 정리하다.

Confusing it with 치우다 — 정리하다 puts things in order in place, while 치우다 clears them away; '치워!' (get it out of here) is harsher than '정리해'.
Assuming it is physical-only — 정리하다 also covers 생각/일정/관계, so 'I need to sort out my schedule' is 일정을 정리해야 돼요, not a cleaning verb.

usage: 문 잠갔어요?
Did you lock the door?
Daily check before leaving home; note the ㅡ drops: 잠그+았 → 잠갔
가스 밸브 잠가 주세요
Please turn off the gas valve
잠그다 also means shutting a valve/tap, not only doors
수도 잠가
Turn off the water
수도(꼭지) = the tap; the casual 'shut the water' between housemates
문 꼭 잠그고 나가세요
Be sure to lock up before you leave
꼭 = without fail; -고 나가다 = lock, then go out
examples: 나갈 때 꼭 문을 잠그세요.
Be sure to lock the door when you go out.
꼭 = without fail; a standard safety reminder for residents
수도꼭지를 안 잠가서 물이 계속 나왔어요.
I didn't turn off the tap so water kept running.
수도꼭지 = faucet; 잠그다 is the verb that pairs with taps
비밀번호로 폰을 잠갔어요.
I locked my phone with a password.
잠그다 extends to locking a phone/screen, not just physical locks
nuance: 잠그다 follows the ㅡ (으-탈락) irregular: the stem vowel 으 disappears before an 아/어 ending, and because the remaining stem vowel ㅏ is 'bright', it joins with 아 — so 잠그 + 아 → 잠가요 and 잠그 + 았 → 잠갔어요 (the 요-form is your anchor: hear 잠가요 and the past, negative, and request forms all fall out). Beyond doors and padlocks it is the standard verb for shutting off water taps and gas valves (수도/가스를 잠그다), which English splits into 'lock' vs 'turn off' but Korean unifies under one image of sealing something closed. Its opposites split too: 열다 (open a door) versus 풀다 (unlock/undo a lock or release). The English-speaker trap is the conjugation: learners regularize it to 잠궈요/잠궜어요, but those are non-standard — the 으 simply drops and ㅏ stays.

Using 끄다 (switch off a device) for a water tap — a faucet or gas valve is 잠그다, while 끄다 is for lights, TVs, and powered machines.
Saying 문을 닫다 when you mean lock — 닫다 only shuts the door; to actually engage the lock you need 잠그다.

usage: 물이 새요
Water is leaking
The first thing to say to the 관리실 about a leak
천장에서 물이 새요
Water is leaking from the ceiling
에서 marks where it leaks from; common in older 빌라
가스가 새는 것 같아요
I think gas is leaking
An urgent line; -는 것 같다 reports a suspected leak you can smell
어디서 새는지 모르겠어요
I can't tell where it's leaking from
-는지 = the indirect 'where/whether'; useful when the source is unclear
examples: 화장실에서 물이 새서 아래층에 피해가 갔어요.
Water leaked from the bathroom and damaged the floor below.
Reporting a serious leak; 아래층 = the floor below you
가스가 새는 것 같아요. 냄새가 나요.
I think gas is leaking. There's a smell.
An urgent pairing; 새다 covers gas leaks as well as water
지붕에서 비가 새요.
Rain is leaking through the roof.
비가 새다 = rain leaking in; the classic monsoon-season problem
nuance: 새다 is intransitive — the liquid, gas, or light is the subject that escapes, so it always takes 이/가 (물이 새다, 가스가 새다, 불빛이 새다), never 을/를; nothing is leaking on purpose. Phonologically the stem vowel ㅐ does not add an extra vowel, it just fuses with the ending: 새 + 었 → 샜어요, 새 + 어요 → 새요. Be careful of the homophone 새다 meaning 'to stay up all night' (밤을 새다 / 밤새다) — that one takes the object 밤, while the leak sense never does, so the particle tells them apart. Compare 흐르다 ('to flow'), which describes liquid moving along a path normally (강물이 흐르다); 새다 specifically means escaping out through a crack, seam, or hole where it should not. The English-speaker trap is treating 'leak' as something you do to an object — in Korean the leaking substance is the grammatical subject.

Mixing it up with 흘리다 ('spill/let flow') — you 흘리다 something on purpose or by accident, but a pipe 새다 on its own; 'the pipe is leaking' is 파이프에서 물이 새요.
Confusing the homophone — 밤을 새다 means staying up all night; a leak never takes 밤 or any object, so keep the particle 이/가.

usage: 빨래 널었어요
I hung up the laundry
A standard chore report; 빨래 = laundry/the wash
빨래 좀 널어 줘
Hang up the laundry, please
A casual request to a roommate or partner; 좀 softens it
빨래 다 마르면 걷어 줘
Take the laundry in once it's dry
걷다 is the partner verb — bring dry laundry back down
햇볕에 널어 둬
Hang it out in the sun (and leave it)
햇볕에 = in the sunlight; -어 두다 = hang it and leave it there
examples: 빨래를 베란다에 널었어요.
I hung the laundry on the balcony.
베란다 = where most Koreans dry clothes; 에 marks the spot
비가 와서 빨래를 못 널어요.
It's raining so I can't hang the laundry out.
못 + verb = unable to; rain blocks line-drying
건조대에 수건을 널어 주세요.
Please hang the towels on the drying rack.
건조대 = clothes drying rack, a household staple
nuance: 널다 is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-탈락) verb: the final ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㄴ, ㅂ, or ㅅ, giving 넙니다 (formal), 너세요 (honorific request), and 너는 빨래 (the laundry being hung) — but it stays before vowel endings, so 너 + 어요 keeps it as 널어요. Its meaning is narrow and physical: spreading out WET laundry on a line, rack, or rail so it air-dries; the partner verb for taking the dry wash back down is 걷다 (빨래를 걷다). Don't confuse it with 말리다 ('to dry something'), which names the result/cause of drying (머리를 말리다 = dry your hair), or with 매달다 ('to hang up by suspending', like a picture or a sign) — 널다 implies laying cloth over something to dry, not hanging an object as decoration. The English-speaker trap is keeping the ㄹ in the formal/honorific forms by analogy with regular verbs.

Using 널다 to hang a picture or coat — that is 걸다 (그림을 걸다, 옷을 걸다); 널다 is specifically spreading wet laundry out to dry.
Mixing it with 말리다 — 말리다 is 'to dry (something)'; you 널어서 말리다, hang it out so that it dries, so the two verbs are not interchangeable.

english: to heat up / to warm up (food)
usage: 전자레인지에 데워 드세요
Heat it in the microwave and eat
What a host or convenience-store clerk might say
국 좀 데워 줄까?
Shall I heat up the soup for you?
A warm domestic offer; 국 = soup
다시 데워 먹어
Reheat it before you eat
다시 데우다 = reheat; -어 먹다 = do it, then eat
우유 데워 줄게
I'll warm the milk up for you
-어 줄게 = I'll do it for you; a caring offer to a child or partner
examples: 남은 밥을 전자레인지에 데웠어요.
I heated up the leftover rice in the microwave.
남은 밥 = leftover rice; 에 marks the appliance used
우유를 따뜻하게 데워 주세요.
Please warm the milk up nicely.
따뜻하게 = so that it's warm; a common adverb with 데우다
찌개를 다시 데워 먹었어요.
I reheated the stew and ate it.
다시 데우다 = reheat; -어 먹다 = do and then eat it
nuance: 데우다 is the transitive 'warm something up' verb, used above all for food and drinks that are already cooked but went cold — leftover rice, soup, milk, a packed meal. Keep three look-alikes apart: 데우다 is the ACTION of heating, 따뜻하다 is an adjective for the resulting STATE ('it's warm'), and 덥다 is an adjective for the weather or your body feeling hot — so '국이 따뜻해요' (the soup is warm) is the result of '국을 데웠어요' (I heated the soup). For raising the food's heat further you choose by method: 끓이다 (boil), 굽다 (grill/roast), 볶다 (stir-fry), 요리하다 (cook generally); 데우다 only brings something back up to a comfortable temperature, it does not cook from raw. The big English-speaker trap is the near-homophone 데다 ('to get burned': 손을 데다 = I burned my hand) — drop one syllable and you change 'heat the food' into 'scald yourself'.

usage: 쓰레기통 좀 비워 줘
Empty the trash can, please
An everyday chore request; 쓰레기통 = trash bin
방을 비웠어요
I cleared out / vacated the room
Also emptying a space when you move out of it
자리 좀 비워 주세요
Please clear the seat/spot
자리를 비우다 = vacate a seat or step away from your place
마음을 비워
Let it go / clear your mind
마음을 비우다 = release expectations; the common figurative use
examples: 음식물 쓰레기통을 비워야 돼요.
I have to empty the food-waste bin.
음식물 쓰레기 = food waste, a separate bin in Korea
냉장고를 비우고 청소했어요.
I emptied the fridge and cleaned it.
-고 links the two chores in the order they happened
이삿날까지 집을 비워 주세요.
Please vacate the apartment by moving day.
집을 비우다 = move out / leave it empty; 이삿날 = moving day
nuance: 비우다 is the causative/transitive partner of the adjective-like verb 비다 ('to be empty'): 비다 describes the state (방이 비었어요 = the room is empty), and you 비우다 something to MAKE it empty (방을 비웠어요 = I emptied the room). So the doer takes the thing as object with 을/를 — a bin, a glass, a fridge, a room. It carries two everyday spins beyond literal emptying: 집을 비우다 / 자리를 비우다 = to be away from home or step away from your seat, and the figurative 마음을 비우다 = to let go of expectations and clear your mind. Its direct opposite is 채우다 ('to fill'). The English-speaker trap is collapsing 'empty the trash' and 'throw away the trash' into one verb: you 비우다 the CONTAINER and 버리다 the CONTENTS — 쓰레기통을 비워서 쓰레기를 버리다 (empty the bin, then throw the trash out), and saying 쓰레기를 비우다 sounds off.

Reading 집을 비우다 only literally — it usually means 'be away from home', so '며칠 집을 비워요' means you'll be out for a few days, not that the house is gutted.

usage: 전구 갈아야 돼요
I need to change the light bulb
전구 = light bulb; 갈다 = swap out a worn part
필터 갈아 주세요
Please replace the filter
Common for 정수기 (water purifier) or AC filters
건전지 갈아 줘
Change the batteries
건전지/배터리 = batteries; 갈다 is the verb for swapping them
새것으로 갈았어요
I replaced it with a new one
새것으로 갈다 = swap for a new one; 으로 marks what it becomes
examples: 화장실 전구를 갈았어요.
I changed the bathroom light bulb.
Object takes 을/를; 전구를 갈다 = replace a bulb
정수기 필터를 6개월마다 갈아야 해요.
You should change the water purifier filter every 6 months.
마다 = every; routine home maintenance
배터리를 새것으로 갈았어요.
I replaced the battery with a new one.
새것으로 갈다 = swap for a new one; 으로 marks the replacement
nuance: 갈다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb (ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ: 갑니다, 가세요, 가는), and in the home sense it means swapping a used-up or worn part for a fresh one — bulbs, filters, batteries, wiper blades, bedsheets (이불을 갈다). Two cautions. First, this 갈다 is a perfect homograph of two other verbs: 갈다 'to grind/whet' (커피를 갈다, 칼을 갈다 = grind coffee, sharpen a knife) and 갈다 'to plough' (밭을 갈다); only context separates them, since the conjugation is identical. Second, distinguish it from 바꾸다 ('to change/exchange'), which is broader and works for swapping anything including abstract things (계획을 바꾸다 = change the plan, 돈을 바꾸다 = exchange money); 갈다 specifically implies replacing a consumable component with an equivalent new one. The English-speaker trap is the ㄹ-irregular: learners write 갈습니다, but the formal form is 갑니다 because ㄹ drops before the ㅂ ending.

usage: 플러그 뽑았어요?
Did you unplug it?
A safety check before leaving; 플러그 뽑다 = unplug
콘센트에서 코드 좀 뽑아 줘
Pull the cord out of the outlet, please
콘센트 = wall outlet (Konglish); 코드 = cord
현금 좀 뽑아 올게
I'll go take out some cash
돈/현금을 뽑다 = withdraw cash from an ATM; very idiomatic
흰머리 뽑지 마
Don't pull out your gray hairs
뽑다 = pluck/pull out; works for hair and weeds too
examples: 외출할 때 가전제품 플러그를 뽑으세요.
Unplug appliances when you go out.
Energy-saving and fire-safety advice; 가전제품 = home appliances
충전기를 콘센트에서 뽑았어요.
I unplugged the charger from the outlet.
에서 marks the place you pull it out of
현금을 좀 뽑아야 돼요.
I need to take out some cash.
돈/현금을 뽑다 = withdraw cash from an ATM, a very common usage
nuance: 뽑다 means pulling something out from where it is set or embedded — a plug from an outlet, but also withdrawing cash from an ATM (돈을 뽑다), plucking a hair, pulling a weed, drawing a number in a lottery, or even selecting/recruiting a person (대표를 뽑다 = pick a representative). Its exact opposite is 꽂다 (to insert/plug in upright). The near-synonym to watch is 빼다 ('to take out/remove/subtract'): both can translate as 'take out', but 뽑다 implies a firm pull against resistance (something was inserted and you yank it free), while 빼다 is gentler removal or extraction (이를 빼다 = have a tooth pulled, 힘을 빼다 = relax/ease off). For plugs and ATM cash specifically, 뽑다 is the idiomatic choice. The English-speaker trap is over-relying on 빼다 for everything 'take out' — for a plug, 코드를 뽑다 sounds far more natural than 코드를 빼다.

Confusing 뽑다 with 꽂다 — they are opposites: 뽑다 pulls out, 꽂다 plugs in; mixing them reverses your meaning entirely.

usage: 플러그 꽂았어요?
Did you plug it in?
Check when an appliance won't turn on; the opposite of 뽑다
콘센트에 꽂아 주세요
Please plug it into the outlet
콘센트 = wall outlet; 에 marks where it goes in
책 책꽂이에 꽂아 줘
Put the book back on the shelf
책꽂이 = bookshelf, literally a 'book-inserting' rack; same verb
충전기 꽂아 놨어
I've left the charger plugged in
-아 놓다/놨다 = did it and left it in that state
examples: 충전기를 콘센트에 꽂았어요.
I plugged the charger into the outlet.
에 marks the destination; the classic plug-in sentence
USB를 노트북에 꽂으면 돼요.
You can just plug the USB into the laptop.
-으면 되다 = it's enough to / just do; 꽂다 fits USB sticks too
꽃을 꽃병에 꽂았어요.
I put the flowers in the vase.
꽂다 also = stand something upright into; 꽃병 = vase
nuance: 꽂다 means inserting something so it stands or stays fixed in place — a plug into an outlet, a USB stick into a port, flowers into a vase, a book into a shelf (hence 책꽂이, 'bookshelf'). It is the natural opposite of 뽑다 (pull out), and it takes the destination particle 에: 콘센트에 꽂다 (into the outlet), versus 뽑다 which takes the source particle 에서. Distinguish it from the broader 넣다 ('to put in/insert'), which just means placing something inside a space (가방에 넣다 = put it in the bag) without the sense of standing it upright or seating it firmly; 꽂다 specifically implies a snug, upright insertion. Two spelling cautions: keep the ㅈ batchim (꽂아요, 꽂습니다 — not 꼽다, which is heard colloquially but is non-standard for this meaning), and don't let the verb 꽂다 blur with the noun 꽃 ('flower'), which sounds nearly the same but is a different word. The English-speaker trap is using 넣다 for plugging in — a plug 'goes into' the outlet, but the idiomatic verb is 꽂다.
